body.en: In a dream-like vision, the speaker, a soldier, seems to escape from battle down a long tunnel, into a dim underworld full of sleeping or groaning figures. One rises and recognises him with pity. This stranger speaks of the hopes he had and the truths about war he could have told the world, which have now died with him; he warns that nations will go on fighting and that the truth will be lost. At the end he reveals that he is the enemy soldier the speaker killed the day before, and he invites him to sleep. The *strange meeting* is between two enemies who are really alike. Read the prescribed text itself; this guide is in our own words and quotes nothing.

body.en: *Strange Meeting* presents war as a waste of young lives and of the hope, beauty and truth they could have given the world. The meeting of enemies shows a common humanity: the "enemy" is a mirror of the speaker, so killing him is a kind of self-destruction. The stranger fears that nations will march on in ignorance, and that the pity of war will go untold. The poem's pararhymes and its unfinished final line leave the reader unsettled, like the war itself. Owen was killed in action in November 1918, a week before the Armistice.

problem.en: Explain the significance of the title Strange Meeting.

steps.en: The meeting is strange because it happens in a dream-like underworld after death.
It is strange because the two men are enemies who meet as friends.
It is strange because the dead man knows the speaker and shares his hopes: they are mirror images.
The title captures the poem's central irony: war makes enemies of people who are alike.

answer.en: The title points to an unnatural, dream-like meeting of enemies who discover their shared humanity.
